entry.evidence: the overall impact of ABCs on the full-waveform inversion problem, from the perspective of computational cost-effectiveness and efficiency, is still widely debated

steps.action: Pose the question of how absorbing boundary conditions affect the full FWI problem, including the adjoint, in effectiveness and computational cost.
steps.quote: the overall impact of ABCs on the full-waveform inversion problem, from the perspective of computational cost-effectiveness and efficiency, is still widely debated

steps.action: Review and adopt published forward formulations of damping, second-order PML, second-order CPML and HABC-A1 as the rival boundary schemes.
steps.quote: Like the damping method, the PML is widely used in seismic problems

steps.action: Construct the new HABC-Higdon scheme: second-order Higdon conditions (angles 0 and pi/4) applied over nested domain extensions with a nonlinear convex weighting.
steps.quote: The method we use in this work employs order 2

steps.action: Derive the adjoint wave equations and adjoint boundary conditions for each ABC (damping, PML, CPML, HABC-A1, HABC-Higdon) via the Lagrangian method.
steps.quote: This derivation shows, once more, the self-adjointing nature of the adjoint problem with HABC-A1 or HABC-Higdon.

steps.action: Implement all forward and adjoint ABCs in Devito with high-level symbolic code, solving the augmented equations only in subdomains of the absorbing region.
steps.quote: The possibility of creating specific subdomains allows us to save time and memory for the computations.

steps.action: Design the test: four heterogeneous velocity models, FWI-type source/receiver layout, reflection-free reference fields on a very large domain, and a relative L2 error on the physical domain.
steps.quote: The goal of this particular and very large extended region is solely to define adequate reference solutions with no inbound reflected waves.

steps.action: Check that the forward and adjoint reference solutions never reach the truncated boundaries, so the reference is free of reflections.
steps.quote: In none of the cases did the waves have time to reach the truncated boundaries

steps.action: Compare forward-solution errors of the five ABCs against the reference across Ricker peak frequencies on the four models; HABC-Higdon has the smallest errors and damping the largest.
steps.quote: It is also clear in Fig. that the HABC-Higdon incurs smaller errors.

steps.action: Vary the extension width p (1 to 20 percent) and peak frequency on Marmousi and SEG/EAGE; errors fall with p and the ranking holds.
steps.quote: In order to ascertain whether similar behaviour would be seen for different sizes of domain extension

steps.action: Compare adjoint-solution errors of the ABCs against a reflection-free adjoint reference; the adjoint has its own boundary reflections plus those carried from the forward solution, and HABC-Higdon is close to or better than PML.
steps.quote: the adjoint problem experiences its own spurious boundary reflections, and those from the forward solution

steps.action: Vary extension width p for several frequencies in the adjoint problem; errors diminish with p for all ABCs, CPML is least effective at high frequency on Marmousi.
steps.quote: In all cases, the error diminishes as p increases.

steps.action: Measure wall-clock time and memory growth of each ABC relative to a no-ABC baseline on Marmousi and plot error against cost; HABC-Higdon is cheaper than PML and CPML at similar error.
steps.quote: HABC-Higdon demands less wall clock time and memory usage than that of PML and CPML

steps.action: Run FWI on the 17 km Marmousi model (f0 = 7 Hz, L-BFGS-B, 40 sources) with damping, PML and HABC-Higdon to estimate the velocity model.
steps.quote: The first case evaluates the ABCs performance in FWI for a fixed peak of frequency

steps.action: Compare misfit, velocity error Ec and cost among ABCs, including damping with a 2.5 km layer; HABC-Higdon gives lower misfit and Ec than PML at lower time cost.
steps.quote: Therefore, it is proper to conclude that HABC-Higdon has shown better overall performance compared to PML.

steps.action: Repeat the FWI comparison at f0 = 15 Hz with a multiscale frequency approach; HABC-Higdon and PML perform similarly (PML lower Ec at 5 and 8 Hz cuts), damping worst.
steps.quote: FWI executions with HABC-Higdon and PML have presented a similar performance.

steps.action: Keep the claim that HABC-Higdon is the most cost-effective ABC among those tested, for forward, adjoint and FWI problems.
steps.quote: On evaluating the computational cost of ABCs methods, HABC-Higdon has shown the best performance

steps.action: Derive expectations, untested here, for 3D cost scaling, real seismograms and other wave physics from symmetry arguments and cited work.
steps.quote: we also expect the effectiveness of the ABCs in 3D problems to be similar to those shown here

steps.action: Referee 1 asked for a bulleted contributions statement; the published introduction lists four contributions as bullets (§1 ¶7).
steps.quote: Could you add a clear "Contributions" section to the paper that highlights (bullet points) what is being claimed as new in this paper?

steps.action: Referee 1 asked how velocity-model choice affects results; the published conclusions add a discussion of incidence angle set by the velocity field (§8 ¶6).
steps.quote: [...] how the choice of velocity models affects the results presented?

steps.action: Referee 1 asked about other physics; the published conclusions add cited expectations for elastic and anisotropic waves (§8 ¶7).
steps.quote: Can you comment on how different physics (e.g. elastic/viscouacoustic) might affect your results?

steps.action: Referee 1 asked whether the adjoint field carries forward reflection errors; the published text states the adjoint carries its own and forward reflections via the forcing term (§6.2 ¶5).
steps.quote: Does the adjoint field include reflection errors from the forward [...] ?

steps.action: Referee 1 asked whether augmented PDEs are solved over the whole domain; the published text describes subdomains where augmented equations are solved only in the extension (§5.1 ¶6).
steps.quote: Are you solving the same augmented PDE in the entire domain (instead of just the boundary region)?

steps.action: Referee 1 asked to distinguish the accuracy reference from the cost baseline; the published text names a separate no-ABC computational reference (§6.3 ¶2).
steps.quote: if the reference/baseline problem has changed between sections, could you please make that more clear.

steps.action: Referee 1 asked to justify subsampling; the published text states the ratios r = 5 and r = 4 satisfy the Nyquist criterion (§7 ¶3, §7 ¶7).
steps.quote: Could you justify the use of subsampling, as well as the chosen subsampling factors?

steps.action: Referee 2 asked to move the adjoint derivations to an appendix; the published paper keeps summary equations in Sect. 4 and full derivations in Appendix A.
steps.quote: the derivations of the ABCs of the adjoint form can be put into an appendex without damaging the main message of this paper

steps.action: Referee 2 asked for FWI results with all ABCs; the published text states FWI was run for all ABCs and models were similar, but plots only damping, PML and HABC-Higdon (§7 ¶9).
steps.quote: I would like to see FWI results for the Marmousi model for all the ABCs that this paper has compared.

steps.action: Referee 2 asked for a figure of staggered-grid variable locations; the published paper includes Figure 2 on PML staggering (§3.3 ¶5).
steps.quote: Can you please add a figure here showing the locations of the staggered grid for different variables in your equation?

end.claim: The proposed hybrid ABC with nested Higdon boundary conditions is as effective as or more effective than PML and the other schemes while being computationally cheaper, making it the most cost-effective ABC tested for FWI.

decisive_move.sentence: Comparing error against wall-clock time and memory for every ABC (Figs. 13-14, Tables 4-5) is what turns the new HABC-Higdon scheme into a cost-effectiveness claim; without it only the construction would exist.

gates.evidence: The stated aim of combining effectiveness with low cost (§1 ¶6) shaped which schemes and measures were run, but no hypothesis directed specific simulations. The headline claim could have failed: HABC-Higdon was compared against PML on error and cost, and PML did give lower Ec at the 5 and 8 Hz cuts (§7 ¶7). Nothing is said to have been fixed before the runs; the extension width was chosen after seeing errors (§6.1 ¶1).

novelty_claims.quote: the HABC-Higdon, first presented in this current work
to the best of our knowledge, those conditions have not yet been assessed for their role in the adjoint problem
There are new implementations of ABCs in Devito, which are openly available for the scientific and industry communities.

limits: The paper reports single deterministic runs; no uncertainty or run-to-run variation of timings is given, and costs come from one machine and one compiler. All data are synthetic; claims for real seismograms, 3D and other wave physics are expectations, not tests (sub-claims at status none). The sub-claim that the adjoint problem has its own boundary reflections is capability_characterized for these models. The HABC-Higdon effectiveness advantage over PML is only partly supported: in the multiscale FWI case PML gave lower velocity error at 5 and 8 Hz cuts. Tuning choices favour the new scheme without fairness checks stated: nonlinear weights were preferred from unshown experiments, alpha follows Liu and Sen, Higdon angles 0 and pi/4 are not justified, and the extension width was chosen to keep errors below a threshold (inference). FWI results for CPML and HABC-A1 are said to be similar but not shown. The review sequence is inferred by matching referee requests to the published text: the authors' responses were in attached zip files not supplied, so whether each change was made in response, or was already present, cannot be confirmed; minor requests (typos, compiler, colour scheme) are not coded. Composition is none_fits: the walk is a method benchmark (question, new method, set computational conditions, comparison against rival methods), with no phenomenon established first as in capability_first and no crucial test with excluding outcomes as in strong_inference.
